extracted.intended_audience: game designers, scholars, critics, and general readers interested in comedy in video games
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for creating and assessing comedic content within video games, covering sources of humor, theoretical approaches, design practices, and reception issues. Targets how narrative, gameplay, and production choices support or undermine comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ludo-comedic consonance
rubrics_metrics.description: "Ludo-comedic consonance", an affinity between narrative and gameplay, reinforces comedy in a similar manner to how ludonarrative dissonance is a disconnect between narrative and gameplay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: ensure narrative and gameplay align to reinforce jokes and comedic situations rather than working at cross purposes. Treat ludo-comedic consonance as a positive design goal analogous to avoiding ludonarrative dissonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources/forms of comedy in games
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy in video games can refer to humorous moments in narrative (such as a witty line of dialog), in gameplay (such as a glitch, explosion, or other event resulting in slapstick humor), or through interacting with the game itself (such as a streamer becoming frustrated at a game).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether humor arises from story/dialogue, emergent/physical gameplay events, or player-mediated interactions (streams, player reactions). Examples: witty dialog (narrative), glitches/slapstick (gameplay), streamer moments (player interaction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary collaboration to create comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: It is often a difficult combined effort between game developers of different disciplines, such as level designers and animators, to make a truly comedic situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: assess cross-disciplinary coordination (design, animation, writing, timing, audio) — comedic beats require synchronized work across teams. Anti-pattern: isolated discipline work that leaves comedic timing or delivery broken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority-based humor
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory of humor in games can be separated into superiority: video games are focused on competition and defeating one's opponent, echoing Plato's association of laughter with hostility towards others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a deliberate comedic mechanism where player triumph, humiliation of opponents, or competitive situations produce humor. Consider ethical implications when humor relies on hostility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity-based humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruity: humor that revolves around how one's expectation does not match the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design surprises, subverted expectations, or mismatched systems to produce comedic effect. Ensure the incongruity is perceivable and contextually supported so it reads as intentional humor rather than a bug.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief/release (comic relief) humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Relief/release: focuses on elements of comic relief, such as sidequests that provide a break from the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use humor as pacing tool to relieve tension — e.g., interstitial side content or lighter scenes that refresh the player. Evaluate placement and frequency to avoid disrupting core gameplay flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing sexuality through humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is commonly used to frame sexuality in video games without being accused of pornography, allowing for transgression of boundaries that would otherwise not be possible, although, in more problematic cases, it has been used to justify highly questionable content (example: Custer's Revenge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: assess whether sexual content is framed as humorous to deflect criticism — weigh artistic intent versus potential for harmful or offensive material. Use caution: humor can enable transgression but also excuse problematic content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of comedy into gameplay (avoid sidelining narrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: As games moved away from text towards emphasis on graphics and action, the story and dialog was 'pushed aside', which can hinder comedy that depends on narrative and dialog.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should integrate comedic writing and narrative earlier and more centrally rather than treating script/dialog as a late add-on. Evaluate whether gameplay decisions support or undermine narrative-based humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Player as the 'straight man' technique
rubrics_metrics.description: One proposed solution is to make the player a 'straight man' to enable comedic contrast and support humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider player positioning and agency so the player reacts to absurdity or comedic NPCs, serving as the foil. Assess whether this role suits the game's mechanical and narrative design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding excessive self-censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Studios self-censored themselves to the point that games were unable to be comedic, out of fear of causing offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: balance risk-taking and sensitivity — evaluate whether fear-driven self-censorship prevents effective comedy. Encourage thoughtful, deliberate risk rather than reflexive removal of potentially funny material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design whole game to support comedy (not one-liners)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy should be a matter of deliberation and thoughtfulness; criticized are games that relied on one-liners and offensive jokes as opposed to designing the entire game to support the comedy. Successful examples cited include Portal 2 and Octodad: Dadliest Catch; Jazzpunk was criticized for lacking 'an emotional core'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: evaluate whether comedic elements are woven into mechanics, pacing, and emotional structure rather than tacked-on jokes. Prefer a coherent emotional core and systemic support for humor over isolated quips or shock jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of writing/script development
rubrics_metrics.description: In most games, a written script is 'considered a late-development afterthought', which can impede comedic effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design guidance: integrate writing and comedic scripting early in development to inform mechanics and level design. Late scripts risk being superficial and out of sync with gameplay.
